items.title: Modern Judaism has Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist branches
items.claim: What distinguishes the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: There are no real denominational differences

Orthodox (Modern Orthodox, Haredi), Conservative (Masorti in UK), Reform, and Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and engagement with modernity

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Modern Orthodox (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging modern life. Haredi (often called 'ultra-Orthodox') resists much of modernity.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as an evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in structurally different ways.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument (1802) was anticipated by Hume's critique
items.claim: What is Paley's design argument and how did Hume respond?

options.text: Paley accepted Hume's criticism and abandoned the design argument

Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) argued from the complexity of a found watch to a designer, by analogy with biology. Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, posthumous) had already attacked the analogy — universe is unlike a watch, the analogy points to an apprentice or committee of designers, not a single benevolent God
Hume defended a stronger version of the argument

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier. Three main lines: the universe is not closely analogous to a watch; the analogy could equally suggest a committee, apprentice or evil designer; the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God of classical theism.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.
